title: Knowing and choosing (5:5)
hook: how can God know and we still choose? God's knowing isn't like ours
tomorrow: can a door close so long it won't open again?

segments.voice: Yesterday: free to choose. Life and good are set before you, not decided for you. Maimonides knew the objection that was coming, and he raises it himself.

The streaming app has the next show lined up before this one ends, and it's annoyingly right. A best friend orders for you at the counter, and gets it exactly. Being known that well can feel cozy, or a little cornering. Now scale it all the way up. If God knows what I'll choose, am I still choosing? One question for today, and Maimonides asks it in his own words before anyone else can.
screen: `THE NEXT SHOW, ALREADY LINED UP.` → `KNOWN THAT WELL.` → `AM I STILL CHOOSING?`

segments.voice: You might ask, he writes: doesn't God know everything before it happens? Then either God knows this person will be righteous, and they can't be otherwise, or they can, and God didn't know. His first answer is honesty: the answer is longer than the earth and wider than the sea. Then the core. People know with a knowledge that's separate from themselves; we and our knowing are two. God and God's knowing are one, and a human mind can't grasp that, just as it can't grasp God. He quotes Isaiah: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways." So we don't know how God knows. But we know without doubt that a person's deeds are in their own hands. Now a neighbor. Boethius, a Christian philosopher, wrote in his Consolation of Philosophy that God sees from an eternal present, and that seeing someone walk doesn't make them walk. What the two share: neither gives up either side. God knows, and we choose, and God's knowing isn't like ours. The honest difference: Boethius offers a picture to help the mind hold it. Maimonides stops on purpose, because any picture would make God's knowing too much like ours. For him, the answer stays beyond our knowing.
screen: `IF GOD KNOWS, CAN I CHOOSE?` · `GOD AND GOD'S KNOWING ARE ONE.` · `BOETHIUS: AN ETERNAL PRESENT.` · `A PICTURE, OR A STOP.` · then, large: `BEYOND OUR KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and hold two sentences side by side, without forcing them to agree: I am known. I am choosing. When the mind tries to solve it, let it rest, and keep both in view until the bell.
Knowing and choosing: Maimonides' answer to the old puzzle. God knows, a person chooses, and how both are true lies beyond our knowing.
For the road: beyond our knowing, and still, your deeds are in your hands. Day fifteen fifty-three, held.

howItsDone: The puzzle of God's knowledge and human choice is studied in Jewish philosophy alongside Pirkei Avot's saying that all is foreseen, yet freedom is given; Maimonides' answer in Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:5 is a classic text for it.
